title: The City Rome Could Not Forgive
hook: Part 7. Why did Rome destroy a city it had already defeated?
full_narration: Part 7. Why did Rome destroy a city it had already defeated? For fifty years, Carthage rose quietly, rich from trade, still paying Rome. [[pause:0.4]] It had no empire, no great army, but its harbor breathed again. On the Numidian frontier, Masinissa pressed Carthaginian land again and again. [[voice:tense]] Rome watched as final judge, while treaty chains made self-defense dangerous. Around 153 BCE, Cato saw Carthage’s wealth and carried fear home. [[pause:0.6]] In Rome, he turned fruit, ships, and silver into a warning. In 151 BCE, Carthage finished its payments, then struck Masinissa without permission. Near Oroscopa, the gamble failed, and Rome received its excuse. [[voice:low]] In 149 BCE, the Third Punic War began against a trapped city. Carthage gave hostages and weapons, but Rome demanded the city move inland. Carthage resisted until 146 BCE; its ruins warned empires what fear remembers. [[pause:0.8]] Follow for the next dark history story.

youtube_description: Part 7 of The Fall of Carthage. After Hannibal’s death, Carthage recovered through trade while still living under Rome’s treaty. But Masinissa pressed its borders, Cato turned its wealth into a warning, and one desperate decision near Oroscopa gave Rome the excuse it wanted. In 149 BCE, the Third Punic War began. Carthage surrendered hostages and weapons, but Rome demanded something deeper: the city must leave the sea. Carthage resisted until 146 BCE, when its fall became a warning about empire, fear, and memory.
